candidates.name: Deirdre Brown
candidates.office: Delegate to the House of Representatives

responses.topThreeActions:
1. Created permanent Statehood infrastructure and institutional commitment at the ward level:
As Chair of the Ward 3 Democratic Committee, I established the Statehood and Home Rule Task Force, ensuring that Statehood advocacy became a standing priority rather than an occasional discussion. I appointed a long standing Statehood advocate to chair the effort, grounding the work in movement leadership. Under my tenure, the Ward 3 Democratic Committee advanced and supported formal resolutions defending DC Statehood and Home Rule in response to congressional interference with the District’s budget and laws. This shifted Statehood from rhetoric to official party action within the ward.

2. Elevated Statehood through sustained public programming and federal engagement:
I coordinated with FreeDC and brought their Campaign Director to address our general body, connecting ward members directly to the broader Statehood campaign. I hosted a town hall with Congressman Jamie Raskin centered on democracy and DC Statehood, strengthening ties between District residents and Congressional allies. I also organized and served as a panelist for a screening of The Last Battlefield, using the discussion to connect the historical roots of disenfranchisement to ongoing congressional efforts to override DC laws and block our budget.

3. Strengthened coalition alignment through the FreeDC Congressional Working Group:
As a member of the FreeDC Congressional Working Group, I work to align ward level organizing with federal advocacy strategy. I coordinated with the Working Group co-leader to deliver a call to action during a Ward 3 Democratic Committee Zoom meeting, ensuring our members were directly mobilized in support of congressional outreach. I consistently frame Statehood as both a democracy issue and a racial justice issue, integrating Home Rule protections into broader conversations about housing, taxation, and local self-governance.
responses.intendedActions:
As the DC Delegate to the US House of Representatives, I will treat DC Statehood as an organizing mandate, not a ceremonial talking point.

First, I will use the office to nationalize the issue. That means consistent engagement with national media, state Democratic parties, and allied members of Congress to ensure DC Statehood remains embedded in the Democratic agenda, particularly during federal election cycles. Statehood cannot disappear between votes.

Second, I will formalize coordination between local leadership and federal advocacy partners. I will work closely with FreeDC, the DC Democratic Party Statehood Committee, Statehood PAC and it’s coalition partners and ward based Democratic organizations to align messaging, rapid response strategy, and congressional outreach. The Delegate’s office should function as a strategic hub for Statehood mobilization.

Third, I will make Home Rule defense immediate and visible. When Congress attempts to interfere with DC laws or block our budget, I will convene public briefings, issue coordinated responses with DC leadership, and activate residents through calls to action that are clear, specific, and measurable.

Finally, I will consistently frame Statehood as a racial justice and democracy issue. The District’s disenfranchisement is not accidental. It is rooted in history, and protecting Home Rule is inseparable from protecting the rights of 700,000 residents to govern themselves.

Statehood requires sustained pressure, disciplined strategy, and coalition strength. I intend to bring all three.
responses.congressResponse:
When Congress attempts to overturn DC laws or block our budget, I will treat it as a direct attack on democratic self-governance, not routine oversight.

First, I will immediately convene a coordinated public response with DC leadership, including the Mayor, Council leadership, and the Attorney General. Within 24 hours, I would call for a joint press conference and issue a unified statement outlining the legal, fiscal, and civil rights implications of the interference.

Second, I would work with the Attorney General and national legal partners to evaluate litigation options, particularly where congressional action violates procedural requirements under the Home Rule Act or constitutional principles. Congressional overreach should be challenged, not absorbed.

Third, I would activate a national advocacy campaign. That means direct outreach to Democratic members of Congress, state party leaders, and allied organizations to force recorded votes and public accountability. I would request meetings with leadership offices and organize coordinated constituent pressure in key states.

Finally, I would ensure residents understand the real consequences. Budget interference delays services, disrupts contracts, and creates instability for working families. I would hold public briefings to explain exactly what is at stake and mobilize residents accordingly.

Congressional interference only continues when it is treated as normal. I will not normalize disenfranchisement.
responses.partners:
1. FreeDC and the FreeDC Congressional Working Group: I have completed the FreeDC orientation and non-cooperation training, and I am a member of the FreeDC Congressional Working Group. I have invited FreeDC leadership to speak at our general body meetings and integrated their calls to action into ward-level organizing. This is an existing strategic partnership that I intend to deepen and scale.

2. DC Democratic Party Statehood Committee:  As Chair of the Ward 3 Democratic Committee, I created a Statehood and Home Rule Task Force to institutionalize advocacy within our ward structure. I intend to work closely with the DC Democratic Party Statehood Committee to align ward level mobilization with citywide party strategy, particularly during federal legislative fights and national election cycles.

3. National Democratic allies in Congress: Through town halls and engagement, including hosting Congressman Jamie Raskin for a Statehood focused discussion, I have built relationships with members of Congress who understand the democracy implications of DC disenfranchisement. As the Delegate, I  will formalize those relationships into coordinated advocacy efforts and ensure that Statehood remains visible within national Democratic caucus conversations.
responses.voterInvolvement:
As an elected official, I will treat DC Statehood as both a federal advocacy responsibility and a sustained organizing mandate.

First, I will maintain a visible and consistent presence on Capitol Hill. I will meet directly with Members of Congress and their staff to educate them on the legal, fiscal, and civil rights implications of congressional interference. I will challenge misinformation about the District and ensure that the realities of governing a majority-Black city without full voting rights are understood clearly. The Delegate’s role requires active engagement, not symbolic representation.

Second, I will institutionalize quarterly town halls focused specifically on Statehood and Home Rule. These forums will provide residents with updates on congressional activity, outline upcoming federal votes, and create structured opportunities for coordinated action. Statehood advocacy should be transparent, regular, and measurable.

Third, I will expand civic education efforts in DC public schools and local universities. The District is home to students from across the country and around the world. I will work with educators and student organizations to ensure that young people understand the limits of Home Rule and the importance of Statehood. When students return to their home states, they should carry that understanding with them.

Fourth, I will strengthen coordination between local leadership and federal advocacy partners. I will work closely with FreeDC, the DC Democratic Party Statehood Committee, ward based Democratic organizations, labor groups, and civil rights allies to align rapid response strategy and congressional outreach. The Delegate’s office should function as a strategic hub for Statehood mobilization.

Finally, when Congress attempts to overturn DC laws or block our budget, I will respond immediately and visibly. That includes coordinated public briefings with DC leadership, direct outreach to congressional offices, and clear calls to action for residents tied to specific legislative timelines.

Statehood requires sustained pressure, disciplined strategy, and public accountability. I intend to bring all three.
responses.additionalComments:
I am a third-generation Washingtonian and a Black woman raising five fourth-generation Washingtonians in this city. My family has paid federal taxes, served this country in the military and as federal workers, built businesses, and invested in our neighborhoods for generations. Yet we remain subject to congressional veto power over our local laws and budget. That is not symbolic. It is structural disenfranchisement.

I want to be clear that my responses reflect how I already operate, not promises I am waiting to keep. I have spent years exposing and challenging systems that fail DC residents, organizing against them when necessary, even when some elected leaders have chosen caution or silence in the face of federal interference. I was taught that change can be driven from the outside or from within institutions, but it requires courage in both spaces. I have organized from the outside. I am ready to take this fight inside the halls of Congress.

As a graduate of the University of the District of Columbia David A. Clarke School of Law, an institution rooted in public service and civil rights, I understand both the legal framework of Home Rule and the historical inequities that continue to shape it. I was trained to use the law as a tool for justice, not a shield for complacency. I am running for Delegate to scale that work, not to soften it.

Too often, DC is represented by candidates who make the right statements about Statehood but hesitate when it is time to speak up, speak out, or resist. Governing requires engagement across differences. It does not require bending the knee in advance, staying silent to preserve access, or accepting federal interference as the cost of doing business. Pre-emptive compliance does not protect DC. It leaves us exposed.

I am committed to resisting injustice rather than normalizing it. That means refusing to legitimize federal overreach, naming harm when it occurs, and organizing collective resistance rather than managing around it. Statehood is not a slogan. It is unfinished civil rights work.

Why me? Because I have already built infrastructure for this fight. I created a Statehood and Home Rule Task Force. I advanced resolutions defending Home Rule. I coordinated with FreeDC and engaged Members of Congress directly. I have organized within ward based Democratic committees, grassroots clubs, and civic networks across the District. I understand that durable political power comes from consistent engagement, not election cycle rhetoric.

At this moment, it matters deeply who is at the table representing DC, locally and nationally. DC does not need the status quo. We do not need empty promises from leaders who have already shown us what they will not do when federal interference occurs. DC needs representation rooted in lived experience, deep community ties, and an unflinching understanding of what federal control costs working families.

If elected, I will treat this office as a platform for defense, resistance, and organizing. I will use it to challenge misinformation, confront federal overreach, and mobilize residents, not to accommodate the status quo.

Representation without resistance is not enough. I am prepared to do both.

candidates.name: Gordon Chaffin
candidates.office: Delegate to the House of Representatives

responses.topThreeActions:
In the 17 years I’ve called D.C. home, I’ve had two distinct activism periods. From 2009 through 2014, I was an ignorant jerk who thought I knew local D.C. because I visited Ben’s Chilli Bowl and read the Prince of Petworth blog. In November 2014, after burning out on a career focused on federal politics, I started listening and reading about the real local D.C. I shut up for five seconds about who I thought should be Senate Majority Leader and learned who John A. Wilson was – and that the building named after him wasn’t “city hall.” As a dog walker running to represent our community in Congress, the long arc of D.C.’s Statehood push forms the connective tissue of roots I’ve set down here 2015 through 2026.

As a transplant to D.C., I’ve passionately argued with fellow young professional transplants – friends, colleagues, and neighbors – that we have an obligation to get involved locally. There are important ways in which we transplants are guests in a fully realized Chocolate City community – and we owe it to our new home that we learn and assist in the long fight for self-government. Sure, it starts with registering to vote here and following the Wilson Building, but it means all the small and large things around that. We should show up to the monthly neighborhood cleanup, we can add our voice to a zoning adjustment case and email our ANC commissioner asking for a provision to the new Settlement Agreement with an ABCA license applicant.

As a local journalist 2017-21, I came to understand and value the ways we could already change our community. D.C. Statehood – the defense and expansion of Home Rule – will be the outcome of decades of civic engagement at all the smaller levels and quieter rooms than the House and Senate floors. Yes, Members of Congress from Hell, Michigan and Winslow, Arizona should hear from their constituents about the need for D.C. We Washingtonians will continue that long campaign, but we need to “act as if” self-government is real now. Because it is!
responses.intendedActions:
Several aspects of Congressional interference in local D.C. life are personal to me. Their budget rider campaigns against D.C. automatic traffic cameras and protected bike lanes threaten my safety. As a dog walker working outside all day, all year, commuting between appointments by e-bike or walking, my physical health is critical. I need streets with safer engineer designs for non-car users and greater enforcement of dangerous driving. It’s hard enough to get through Wednesday gauntlets – sometimes with 10 dog walk appointments – without needing to keep 100% maximum vigilance because drivers are reckless.

As Delegate, I would fight back against budget riders and standalone non-budget legislation that overrule local decision-making – even when I personally disagree with Council and Mayoral calls. I would also work to move beyond the constant trench fighting in these riders and bills. D.C. residents and business owners, visitors to the District, would have to follow different rules every 3-6 months based on the whims of Members of Congress from who knows where. If Republicans retain Congressional control, I would try to convince my colleagues across the aisle to at least give us a set of clear, consistent guidelines for doing business and raising kids as D.C. denizens.

I see the next Delegate’s self-government and autonomy defense portfolio as shaped largely by the results of November 2026’s General Election. Democrats must win back both chambers of the Congress in November 2026 with majorities where statehood bills have a reasonable chance for success. Our next Delegate must work hard on the campaign trail to make sure Democrats nominate the best 2028 Presidential candidate and win back the White House. The 2029 Congressional Session, with a trifecta, is the realistic D.C. Statehood timeline.
responses.congressResponse:
As a local journalist in 2020, I covered the George Floyd uprising here in the District and the public outcry that became D.C. Council legislation on public safety reforms. I remember how strange it was to watch federal law enforcement clear H Street NW of protestors – a public space owned and operated by D.C. – so that President Trump could incorrectly hold a Bible amid lingering counter protest aerosol smoke.

As Delegate, I would fight to defend all local D.C. laws and budget decisions. My personal public policy positions would be subordinate to the demonstrated will of our neighbors made extant with Wilson building decision making. This includes items like the STEER Act with its legal modifications for greater traffic safety and the SECURE DC law, both passed in 2024.
responses.partners:
Speaking as a Free DC trainee, that young movement is an obvious partner to promote self-government expansions toward Statehood and defend Home Rule. I would work to assist and augment whatever Capitol Hill activities Free DC plans and coordinate with their “off-campus” efforts in virtual and real life settings. I appreciate Free DC’s coherent vision and research-backed plan pushing toward Statehood.

In following public reports of recent Hill advocacy activities from sitting local D.C. elected officials, it has appeared from the outside to be disjointed and flailing. As Delegate, I would push for a unified Hill advocacy strategy among all of the local D.C. decision makers. I don’t want to be a micro-manager, I don’t need to be the loudest or longest voice at the press conferences. But, I would work as Delegate so that we all aren’t getting on phone calls undermining each other.
responses.voterInvolvement:
D.C. residents are the best voice promoting Statehood, and defending our Home Rule autonomy in the meantime. A lesson of the Free DC Movement from that group’s young tenure is that regular people are the most persuasive folks to walk House and Senate office buildings. Important adults in suits with glossy, high-contrast infographics and “one sheets” are a dime-a-dozen on Capitol Hill. I would listen to and give more microphones to the families where Home Rule defense means improvements to daily life.

As Delegate, I would step in wherever and however my office could augment the preexisting grassroots efforts. I would carry the voice and authority of that office, but I don’t think the Delegate should try to reinvent the wheel from D.C.’s Mayoral, Council, and non-government group activism. I’m energy where our residents need energy, strategic guidance when that would be helpful, and a bully pulpit user (pulpit-eer?) at a lectern carrying the U.S. House seal.
responses.additionalComments:
The long fight for a moral absolute – the case for D.C. Statehood – is why I set down roots in the District. I want to be a founding resident of the Douglass Commonwealth.

A 1993 event flyer I have framed says “the time has come to accelerate the drive for Statehood” in its advertisement of a “We Love D.C. Gala Performance.” Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton co-chaired the gathering, shortly after getting the first-ever committee hearing for D.C. Statehood. Jesse Jackson is also listed as a co-chair above his title as D.C. Shadow Senator. The flyer lists Vice Chairs including Marion Barry and Harry Thomas Sr. I am moved by these legacies – they are the cornerstones of our movement toward Statehood and we stand firmly as we push toward 1 million residents as the 51st U.S. state.

candidates.name: Samuel Greenfield
candidates.office: Delegate to the House of Representatives

responses.topThreeActions:
Over the past two years, three actions stand out as especially meaningful in advancing DC Statehood:

1. Elevating Public Awareness Nationwide
I’ve consistently highlighted the case for DC Statehood in discussions, educational content, and civic conversations—helping explain why over 700,000 residents of Washington, D.C. deserve full voting representation in Congress. Increasing general understanding is foundational to building sustained national support.

2. Supporting Legislative Momentum
I’ve helped clarify and communicate the details and significance of the Washington, D.C. Admission Act, including what statehood would mean for representation, budgeting, and local autonomy. Clear explanations help more people engage meaningfully with the policy itself rather than just the politics around it.

3. Centering Democratic Principles
I’ve emphasized the broader constitutional and civil rights arguments—framing DC Statehood as an issue of equal citizenship and democratic fairness. By grounding the conversation in shared democratic values, it strengthens long-term advocacy efforts beyond any single news cycle.
responses.intendedActions:
As a DC elected official, I would focus on five key actions to advance Statehood and protect Home Rule:

1. Push for passage of the Washington, D.C. Admission Act by working closely with the United States Congress. 

2. Defend the District of Columbia Home Rule Act by opposing congressional attempts to overturn locally passed laws.

3. Mobilize residents and national allies to frame Statehood as a civil rights and democracy issue.

4. Protect DC’s budget autonomy to reduce federal interference in locally raised funds.
Prepare operationally for Statehood to ensure a smooth transition when enacted.

DC residents deserve full representation and control over their own laws.
responses.congressResponse:
If elected, I will defend the right of the people of the District of Columbia to govern themselves.

If United States Congress attempts to overturn DC laws or block the budget, I would publicly oppose the action and I would take three specific actions:

1. Formally oppose and lobby against disapproval resolutions in the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate, organizing a rapid-response coalition to stop them before passage.

2. Pursue legal action by directing the DC Attorney General to challenge any overreach in federal court.

3. Push for permanent reform, including passage of the Washington, D.C. Admission Act and stronger local budget autonomy protections.

My priority would be defending DC’s right to govern itself.
responses.partners: The top partners I plan to engage in promoting DC statehood include my colleagues in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, as well as national and local advocacy organizations that have long championed this cause, such as DC Vote and other civic groups. By combining these legislative and grassroots partnerships, I aim to build momentum and foster bipartisan support for the District of Columbia Admission Act (S. 51). I also maintain professional relationships with several congressional staffers whose members support DC statehood, which will help advance these efforts.
responses.voterInvolvement:
To involve D.C. voters and residents in the fight for Statehood, I would focus on three priorities:

1. Educate and Inform
Host ward-based forums explaining how lack of statehood affects taxation, budget control, and representation in the United States Congress. Share clear comparisons showing that states like Wyoming have full representation while D.C. does not.

2. Mobilize Grassroots Action
Build neighborhood-based Statehood Action Teams, partner with local organizations, and work closely with leaders to connect residents directly to federal advocacy efforts.

3. Engage Youth and Community Voices
Activate students at institutions such as Howard University and empower young leaders to drive digital campaigns, rallies, and storytelling initiatives.

The goal is to make statehood personal, visible, and community-led—so residents aren’t just supporting the movement, but shaping it.
responses.additionalComments:
I strongly support DC statehood because the more than 700,000 residents of the District pay federal taxes, serve in the military, and fulfill all the responsibilities of citizenship — yet they lack full voting representation in Congress. That fundamental imbalance contradicts the democratic principles our nation claims to uphold.

For decades, residents of Washington, D.C. have been denied voting representation in the United States Congress, despite having a population larger than several existing states. The rallying cry on DC license plates — “Taxation Without Representation” — is not symbolic; it reflects a real democratic deficit.

Statehood would:
1. Provide two U.S. Senators and at least one voting Representative.
2. Grant full local autonomy over budgeting and laws.
3. Ensure DC residents have equal standing with citizens in all 50 states.

I believe DC statehood is not a partisan issue — it is a fairness issue. If we believe in government by the people, then we must ensure all Americans have an equal voice in that government.

DC voters deserve nothing less than full democracy.

responses.topThreeActions: This is a crisis moment for DC - and it’s why I decided to step up and run for Congress in the first place. The first action I’m proudest of is fighting back against the decision to revoke DC’s sanctuary city status. After the Mayor decided to repeal DC’s sanctuary values law, I led the fight to place it back into the budget - and we won. Second, I’m using my position as Chair of the Council Committee on Public Safety and the Judiciary to ensure that DC residents have transparency and accountability from our MPD and federal law enforcement operating here. That’s why I introduced a body worn camera bill in February, to ensure that when federal officers engage in a violent incident, that footage must be released to the public. Finally, I’ve been on Capitol Hill nearly every week since Donald Trump’s inauguration championing the case of DC’s self-determination in Congress, making sure that members of both parties understand the consequences of their actions for the safety and livelihoods of DC residents.
responses.intendedActions: As a current member of the DC Council, I’m fighting every single day to protect Home Rule. I’m very proud of the work of my office to protect DC’s sanctuary city law, even in the face of threats from the Trump Administration.
responses.congressResponse: In Congress, it will be my job to protect every DC law passed by our DC Council - because my job is to protect our democracy, not pick and choose which laws I support and overturn the ones I don’t. I’ll use my committee assignments and office to make the case to all my colleagues about the impacts of their legislation, and I’ll campaign across the country to build a pro-statehood majority in Congress so we never have to be held hostage to the whims of Congress again.
responses.partners: First, local activists who have made this fight a reality for the last several decades, including the DC Democratic Party and the DC Statehood PAC. Second, I believe that we need to build a national movement to elect a pro-statehood majority to the House and Senate - so I’ll work with progressive allies in every corner of the country to elect federal officials who will center DC Statehood in their campaigns.
responses.voterInvolvement: Every single issue facing our city today - from our Medicaid allocation, to funding for our schools, to police presence in our streets - is a function of DC’s lack of statehood. I’ll plan to regularly convene advocates on all of these issues to strategize on how to build national power for a pro-statehood majority in the Senate and the House nationally.
responses.additionalComments: Every single issue facing our city is exacerbated due to our lack of statehood and voting representation in Congress. We need to build a national movement to elevate this issue to the top of the Democratic agenda in every single federal race across the country so we can build a pro-statehood majority in the House and Senate.

Hosted Zoom calls to drive early voter engagement and voter registration to counter the impact of the SAVE Act (if passed by the Senate). I focused these calls on protecting ballot access and preventing disenfranchisement that would weaken our ability in DC and nationally to elect representatives who support DC Statehood and defend Home Rule.

As a member, I support a mission focused on empowering Black women to drive policy, support candidates who back DC Statehood, and build durable, cross-industry relationships that strengthen organizing capacity and sustained advocacy.
responses.intendedActions:
As a DC elected official, I will pursue a “pressure + participation + protection” strategy:

Pressure Congress with organized, timed resident action tied to Congressional calendars, including rapid mobilization when interference bills move and coordinated outreach to key Senate and House targets.

Expand civic education and voter engagement at scale, building on my webinars and Zoom trainings by launching a consistent schedule of Statehood teach-ins, registration and engagement drives, and “how Congress impacts DC” briefings.

Nationalize the DC Statehood case by leveraging cross-state relationships and national networks to make DC Statehood a democracy priority beyond the District, not just a local issue.

Build durable coalitions that center Black women and community leadership, including continuing active engagement with Win With Black Women to support candidates and policies that advance Statehood and defend Home Rule.

Keep DC residents in the driver’s seat through ward-based organizing, transparent updates, and easy-to-use action tools so residents always know: what’s happening, what it means, and what to do next.
responses.congressResponse:
Specific action: I will activate a 24-hour Home Rule Rapid Response that includes a public briefing, coordinated press with coalition partners, and a resident action push targeted at the Members of Congress driving the interference.

That includes:

A district-targeted pressure plan (calls, visits, emails, earned media, and partner mobilization) aimed at the Senate/House decision-makers.

A public “harm receipt” explaining what interference will cost DC residents in real terms (services, public safety, schools, and local economic stability).

Coordination with legal and civil rights partners when appropriate to support challenges and protect DC’s democratic rights.

Congressional interference is not theoretical. Recent federal action to block DC’s local tax changes is one example of how Congress can undercut DC’s autonomy and budget choices.

responses.voterInvolvement:

Ward-based Statehood teams with monthly goals (registration, turnout, outreach, teach-ins, Congressional pressure).

responses.additionalComments:
DC Statehood is a civil rights issue and a democracy issue. Home Rule is not enough when Congress can override DC laws and control DC’s budget. The only lasting solution is full Statehood and equal representation.

I also believe the fight for Statehood is inseparable from protecting voting access nationwide. Efforts like the SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, risk creating barriers that could disenfranchise eligible voters and weaken our ability to elect Statehood champions.

responses.topThreeActions:
As a concern citizen of the United states of American, I asked the question, what is the real reason the residents of the district of Columbia are denied federal representation although DC consistently ranks first for individual federal income and payroll taxes, often with per-capita contributions that are double or more the national average. From a human perspective, this doesn’t seem fair. I Followed the Supreme Court’s rulings regarding DC Statehood

1. D.C. is Not a Constitutional "State"

Case Reference: Hepburn v. Ellzey (1805) and Adams v. Clinton (2000).

The Ruling: While D.C. is a "distinct political community," it is not one of the "states" of the Union. Because the Constitution specifically grants House and Senate seats to states, D.C. does not qualify for them under its current status.

2. Residents Have No Constitutional Right to Vote in Congress

Case Reference: Castañon v. United States (2021).

responses.intendedActions:
As Mayor, I will make expanding the rights of DC residents a governing priority - not just through the fight for statehood, but by exploring every available avenue to secure representation while that longer fight continues.

Statehood remains the goal. Full statehood is the only complete solution as it gives DC residents congressional voting power. I will sustain that fight with dedicated staff, national advocacy, and coordination with our next Congresswoman and our Shadow delegation. But I will also pursue interim paths to representation.  Specifically, I will work with Congressional allies to revive efforts to secure a voting House member for DC without requiring full statehood. Here's how that could work:

The DC House Voting Rights Act approach: Congress has considered legislation that would grant DC a voting representative in the House by statute. Previous versions (2007, 2009) passed the House but stalled in the Senate. These bills treated DC "as though it were a state" for purposes of House representation, relying on Congress's broad authority under the District Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 17). Past versions paired DC's seat with an additional seat for a Republican-leaning state to build bipartisan support. As Mayor, I will actively lobby for renewed Congressional action on this approach.

Critics argue that Article I limits House membership to "the several States," meaning only a constitutional amendment can grant DC a House vote. Supporters counter that the District Clause gives Congress plenary authority over DC, including the power to treat it as a state for specific purposes—as we already do for federal programs, judicial proceedings, and other matters. This is a live legal debate, and I believe DC should force the question rather than accept disenfranchisement as permanent.

A targeted constitutional amendment: If the statutory path faces insurmountable legal challenges, a constitutional amendment focused solely on House representation could be considered. The 23rd Amendment (giving DC electoral votes) passed in 1961 with bipartisan support because it was narrowly tailored. A similar amendment for House representation could potentially attract support from members who aren't ready for full statehood but recognize the injustice of total disenfranchisement.

Statehood is the right answer. But DC residents have been waiting for representation since 1801. As Mayor, I will pursue every constitutionally available path—statutory, legal, and political—to expand our rights while the statehood fight continues. We should not let the perfect be the enemy of progress.

Some members of Congress oppose DC statehood because they believe it would change the balance of representation in the Senate. That means we must be open to creative solutions that advance democracy while addressing political concerns. One idea that has been discussed nationally is pairing DC statehood with Puerto Rico statehood and admitting both jurisdictions as states at the same time. Historically, the United States has admitted states in pairs to address political balance concerns. Approaches like this may help break the current gridlock and move the conversation forward.

Community Advocacy: He emphasizes using his "Enforcer" reputation to fight for local control and ensure D.C. residents have a primary voice in their city's future.
Grassroots Mobilization: His campaign utilizes grassroots activities to engage voters directly on issues of local sovereignty and economic stability. 
Specific Actions to Promote D.C. Statehood

D.C. leaders are taking the following legislative and advocacy steps in 2025 and 2026:
The Washington, D.C. Admission Act (H.R. 51): Reintroducing and championing this bill to admit the residential areas of D.C. as the 51st state (the Douglass Commonwealth) while maintaining a smaller federal district for government buildings.

D.C. Statehood Pledge: Mobilizing candidates and elected officials to sign the D.C. Statehood Pledge, committing to the formal admission of D.C. into the Union.
National Education Campaigns: Using the upcoming U.S. 250th anniversary in 2026 as a platform to highlight the lack of voting representation for D.C.’s 700,000 residents. 
Protecting Home Rule from Federal Interference

In response to "attacks on limited Home Rule" in 2025 and early 2026, officials are focused on:
The District of Columbia Legislative Home Rule Act: Supporting federal legislation (like H.R. 214) designed to eliminate Congress's authority to nullify locally enacted D.C. laws.
Defending Local Prosecution Power: Opposing efforts to strip the D.C. Attorney General of power and fighting for the transfer of local prosecution authority from the federal U.S. Attorney’s Office to local control.

Police and Guard Autonomy: Advocating for the repeal of Section 740 of the Home Rule Act, which allows the President to seize control of the Metropolitan Police Department during "emergencies," and seeking mayoral control over the D.C. National Guard.

responses.topThreeActions:
We are witnessing nothing short of an assault on DC's democracy and autonomy. These actions are completely unacceptable, unnecessary, costly, and unconstitutional. They represent creeping fascism that threatens not just DC residents' ability to govern ourselves, but the safety, dignity, and fundamental rights of our most vulnerable neighbors—particularly our immigrant communities who are being terrorized by ICE raids and deportations.

As an ANC1E Commissioner I voted consistently in support of Statehood and in opposition to federal overreach. That included (1) opposition to Congressional interference with 16 bills to roll back DC laws and (2) support for the swift adoption of the DC budget without Congressional interference as well as (3) resolutions affirming Sanctuary City status. On a personal note, joining Statehood actions with Free DC has been a particularly meaningful way to be in community with other Ward 1 residents.
responses.intendedActions:
The role of Councilmembers in resisting this federal overreach is not passive—it requires bold, strategic, and relentless action. As Ward 1 Councilmember, I will approach this fight on multiple fronts:
First and most importantly, I will continue standing and speaking out against Trump and federal interference at every opportunity and publicly denouncing his actions. While silence can be viewed as strategic, I see it as complicity. DC residents deserve a Councilmember who will name what we're facing: fascism, white supremacy, and authoritarian federal overreach that treats DC residents as second-class citizens without full democratic rights. I will use my platform to make clear that these actions are attacks not just on local autonomy but on the fundamental principles of democracy and self-governance. As Councilmember, I do not support our community being terrorized and will use fierce resistance and my legislative powers and organizing skills to fight back!

Second, I will use the Council's legislative powers to close loopholes in local law that allow for inappropriate cooperation with federal authorities like ICE. DC has declared itself a sanctuary city, but that commitment means nothing if local agencies and resources are being used to facilitate deportations and immigration enforcement. I will introduce or co-sponsor legislation that: explicitly prohibits DC government employees and agencies from cooperating with ICE except where absolutely required by law; prevents the use of DC resources, facilities, or personnel to support federal immigration enforcement; strengthens protections for sensitive locations like schools, hospitals, and places of worship; and creates penalties for violations of these policies. 

Third, I will use the Council's oversight and investigative powers to document federal overreach and hold hearings that expose the human cost of these attacks. I will demand that DC agencies report on every instance of federal interference: How many times has ICE requested cooperation? How are federal deployments of the National Guard affecting public safety and community trust? What is the fiscal impact of blocked budget funds on critical services? What legal violations are occurring? These hearings will serve multiple purposes: creating a public record of federal abuses, amplifying the voices of residents directly harmed, building political pressure for resistance, and identifying specific areas where local action is needed. I will invite legal experts, immigrant rights advocates, constitutional scholars, and most importantly, DC residents experiencing this persecution to testify and share their stories.

Fourth, I will advocate for dedicating DC government resources to legal challenges against unconstitutional federal actions. The Office of the Attorney General should be filing lawsuits challenging every significant federal overreach—from budget blocks to forced cooperation with immigration enforcement to violations of the Home Rule Act. I will use my budget powers to ensure the OAG has adequate resources for this litigation.  Attorney General Brian Schwalb has already filed multiple lawsuits challenging Trump administration overreach, including suits against the attempted federal takeover of MPD and the deployment of National Guard troops in the District, which he has described as an illegal "military occupation." His office has argued that these federal actions violate the Home Rule Act and represent "the gravest threat to Home Rule that the District has ever faced." As Councilmember, I will ensure that the OAG has robust budget allocations to continue and expand this critical litigation, recognizing that legal challenges are one of our most powerful tools for protecting DC autonomy. I will also use my oversight powers to publicly support AG Schwalb's efforts, amplify the cases he's bringing, and pressure the Mayor and other agencies to fully cooperate with legal strategies to resist federal overreach. The Attorney General cannot fight these battles alone—he needs the full backing of the Council, adequate resources, and coordinated action across DC government.
 
Fifth, I will work to ensure that DC government actively protects residents rather than passively allowing federal persecution. This means: creating emergency funds to support residents facing deportation or federal prosecution; ensuring that DC's identification programs remain accessible to all residents regardless of immigration status; maintaining and expanding language access so that non-English speakers can access services and know their rights; and using every available tool in local government to create barriers to federal enforcement and sanctuaries for vulnerable residents. Because Ward 1 has the highest concentration of immigrant residents in the city, I will leverage my Council position to ensure that our non-profit organizations who protect and serve our immigrant neighbors are well-resourced and represented by their elected officials. We should have their back and demonstrate that with our legislative and budgetary power and authorities!
responses.congressResponse: I will work directly with Members of Congress who support DC statehood and autonomy to build federal legislative strategies to protect our self-governance. While we cannot rely on Congress to save us—particularly under Republican control—we must maintain relationships with allies who can introduce legislation, use committee hearings to expose abuses, and build public pressure. My seven years as a registered federal lobbyist gave me experience navigating Capitol Hill, building relationships with congressional staff, and understanding how to influence federal policy even from disadvantaged positions. I will leverage these skills to advocate for DC autonomy, budget release, and legislative protections against federal overreach.
responses.partners: I will partner with legal clinics and nonprofit organizations with experience in organizing campaigns to mobilize, educate, and train DC residents to know their rights and protect themselves from lack of due process and harm. This includes: funding and promoting know-your-rights trainings, particularly for immigrant communities; supporting legal defense funds and rapid response networks that can intervene when ICE conducts raids; ensuring that DC residents understand their Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches and seizures; and building community defense networks where neighbors look out for each other. My decade of community organizing through Georgia Avenue Thrive taught me that residents with knowledge and collective power can resist even well-resourced oppression. We must build infrastructure that allows our community to protect itself, not wait for government institutions to save us.
responses.voterInvolvement: As a Ward 1 resident for over 20 years and ANC Commissioner for a decade, I've walked these streets not as a policymaker observing from afar, but as a neighbor, a community organizer, and someone deeply invested in the safety and well-being of every person who calls our ward home. I co-founded and led what is now Georgia Avenue Thrive—a community led initiative evolving from a public safety taskforce that brought together residents, small businesses, and local government to address safety concerns not through increased policing, but through community activation, economic development, and collaborative problem-solving. I've seen firsthand that real community comes from investment in people and neighborhoods. DC is under attack by President Trump and Congress right now, and now is the time to come together and fight together.
responses.additionalComments:
As a candidate for DC Council in Ward 1, I am deeply alarmed by what we are witnessing — not just here in DC, but in cities across this country. We are watching democratic norms erode in real time. We are seeing the will of voters undermined, local decision-making attacked, and power consolidated in ways that silence communities instead of uplifting them.

And I’m angry.

I’m angry because the people who bear the brunt of democratic backsliding are Black and Brown residents — the very communities who have fought hardest to expand access to the ballot, to housing, to safety, to education, to opportunity. In DC, a majority-Black city with no full voting representation in Congress, our lack of statehood is not an accident. It is the result of unbalanced power rooted in structural racism — a system that has long been comfortable controlling Black political power while denying Black political self-determination.

When local decisions are overridden, when budgets are interfered with, when our autonomy is treated as conditional, it sends a clear message: our democracy is fragile, and it is not distributed equally.

We cannot separate today’s democracy crisis from white supremacy. White supremacy is not just about hate; it is about power — who holds it, who protects it, and who is denied it. Structural racism has shaped whose voices are centered and whose are dismissed. And when democracy weakens, those already pushed to the margins are the first to feel the impact.

What we are dealing with today isn’t new. It has always existed in different forms — voter suppression, disenfranchisement, redlining, over-policing, economic exclusion. What’s different is the face it wears and the boldness with which it operates at a time when we should be progressing, not moving backwards as we are today.
But history also teaches us something else: when democracy is threatened, people organize. People build. People fight forward.
It’s time to level the playing field so all people can win. It’s time to strengthen local power, protect our rights, fight for statehood and ensure that DC residents have full voice and representation.

Let’s free DC. 

Thank you for your consideration!

responses.voterInvolvement: I intend to involve D.C. voters and residents by making Statehood and Home Rule a visible, ongoing part of local civic engagement, not an abstract issue discussed only when Congress intervenes. I will work through ANCs, community associations, and advocacy partners to provide clear, accessible information about how the lack of Statehood directly affects residents’ services, taxes, and local decision-making. I will also use public meetings, neighborhood forums, and direct outreach to create opportunities for residents to ask questions, share concerns, and participate in coordinated advocacy when Home Rule is threatened.
responses.additionalComments: DC Statehood is not a symbolic issue to me. It is about whether more than 700,000 District residents are treated as full citizens with the right to govern ourselves. Protecting Home Rule and advocating for Statehood are pillars of my campaign because they affect every issue we care about, from public safety to our locally raised tax dollars. I will treat Statehood not as a talking point, but as an ongoing responsibility and a core part of fighting for dignity, autonomy, and equal representation for the people of the District.

responses.topThreeActions:
Over the last almost four years, I am most proud of three actions I have taken in support of DC Statehood. First, I have consistently fought against congressional interference in our local laws, using my vote and my voice to defend the District’s autonomy whenever Congress attempted to override the will of DC residents. Protecting Home Rule is foundational to the broader fight for statehood.

Second, I have used my platform to actively educate leaders and audiences outside of DC about why statehood is a matter of civil rights, democracy, and racial equity. Whether in national forums, meetings with stakeholders, or public commentary, I have made clear that taxation without representation is unacceptable in 2026.

Third, I have publicly and unequivocally endorsed DC Statehood as a policy priority, integrating it into my advocacy rather than treating it as symbolic rhetoric. Statehood is not an abstract issue. It is about full voting representation, budget autonomy, and self-determination for our residents, and I will continue advancing that fight both inside and outside the District.
responses.intendedActions: I have and intend to hold the line aggressively against congressional interference, including in the current tax fight. When Congress attempts to overturn or undermine locally enacted revenue measures, I will use every available platform to defend the District’s authority to govern its own budget and tax policy.
responses.congressResponse:
When Congress has attempted to overturn DC laws or interfere with our budget, I have responded immediately and publicly. I have educated residents about what was at stake through town halls, media appearances, and direct communication, making clear how congressional interference harms DC families in real and tangible ways. I have worked with my Council colleagues to pass formal resolutions rejecting interference and affirming our commitment to Home Rule.

I have also lobbied members of Congress, met with federal offices, and partnered with national civil rights and democracy organizations to build opposition to these efforts. When necessary, I have supported exploring legal strategies through the Attorney General. I have refused to normalize interference as routine, and I will continue using my voice and my office to defend DC’s autonomy and advance Statehood.
responses.partners:
In promoting DC Statehood, I intend to continue working closely with our Delegate to Congress, our Shadow Representative and Shadow Senators, and the DC Democratic Party.

I have an active working relationship with our Delegate’s office and have partnered on messaging and advocacy when Congress has attempted to interfere with DC laws or our budget. I have also engaged with our Shadow delegation to amplify statehood education efforts and align local and national advocacy strategies. In addition, I have worked with leaders within the DC Democratic Party to elevate Statehood as a core civil rights and democracy issue in local and national political spaces. These relationships are ongoing and collaborative, and I will continue strengthening them to ensure our push for Statehood is coordinated, visible, and persistent.
responses.voterInvolvement:
I believe Statehood will only be won if DC residents are organized, informed, and mobilized. I have already worked to educate voters about congressional interference and what it means for our budget, our laws, and our rights. Most recently, I led a delegation of nearly 50 Ward 5 neighbors to Capitol Hill to meet directly with Members of Congress and their staff to lobby against harmful congressional action. That kind of direct civic engagement matters. It shows that DC residents are not passive observers. We are active participants in defending our democracy.

Going forward, I will continue hosting town halls, organizing advocacy days, and partnering with civic and community organizations to equip residents with the tools to contact Congress, submit testimony, and elevate their voices nationally. Statehood cannot just be a slogan from elected officials. It must be a people powered movement. My role is to educate, convene, and mobilize residents so they are empowered to demand full representation and self determination.
responses.additionalComments:
Now more than ever, DC needs serious, steady leadership in the face of unprecedented congressional interference and political uncertainty. Statehood is not a symbolic issue for me. It is about protecting our budget, our public safety laws, our healthcare programs, and our fundamental right to self governance. Given the level of change and disruption facing the District, we must rely on experienced, proven leaders who understand both the policy and political terrain and who believe deeply in Statehood as a matter of civil rights and democracy.

I have not wavered on this issue. I have fought against congressional overreach, educated audiences inside and outside the District, mobilized residents to advocate on the Hill, and used my platform to center Statehood in the broader national conversation. DC voters deserve representation that is consistent, informed, and unafraid to defend our autonomy. I remain fully committed to that fight.

responses.topThreeActions: I have been a consistent and fierce advocate for full DC Statehood over the years. I’ve met directly with numerous members of Congress and Democratic House leadership, I’ve walked side-by-side with DC residents advocating and educating members of Congress, and I’ve joined public rallies to declare clearly and loudly why DC Statehood is needed now more than ever. I’ve also defended Council-passed laws under threat from the Trump Administration and Congress.
responses.intendedActions: I have consistently and fiercely defended DC Statehood for years. I have worked to develop relationships with members of Congress to help educate them about the importance of DC Statehood and to be our champions. I will also continue to be active in resident actions at the Capitol and elsewhere to join grassroots movements fighting for DC Statehood. And when Home Rule or DC laws are threatened, I won’t stay silent or sit out the fight. As I have demonstrated, I will speak out and show up to declare clearly and loudly why DC Statehood is needed now more than ever.
responses.congressResponse: As a current elected official, I use my position to speak loudly against any and all congressional attempts to overturn DC laws and encourage residents to make their voices heard. I have defended the District’s laws and local control. Not every DC elected official has shown up when it mattered, but I have. Throughout the past 12 months, I’ve worked strategically to push the Council to bring on advocacy capacity, lobby members of Congress, partner with advocacy efforts like Free DC, and use the power of my office to speak in press, public appearances, and directly to my constituents about why action must be taken to defend the District of Columbia.

These actions cannot be done only when it’s easy or convenient, but elected officials must demonstrate the courage to show up and speak out every day and in every fight.
responses.additionalComments: I try to never miss an opportunity to advocate for DC Statehood. Whether it’s addressing a convention of out-of-town visitors or elected colleagues, or sitting down with our local Scouts or school children, educating and advocating for DC Statehood - and highlighting the inherent injustice that still exists today - must be part of every engagement strategy. It was even my legislation the Council passed to change DC’s license plates to read “End Taxation Without Representation” - to remind everyone that statehood and autonomy will only be won through action, strategy, and organizing.

responses.topThreeActions:
1. I have been an active member of the Free DC movement and other local efforts to defend Home Rule and advance DC Statehood, including public demonstrations, press conferences, lobby days, coalition calls, and organizing meetings.

2. Joined the board of DC Statehood PAC to advance our federal fight for self-determination, directing funds to congressional candidates in support of the Washington DC Admission Act.

3. Been an effective spokesperson to media, helping to shape the local and national narrative in the midst of attacks on DC's Home Rule under both the Biden and Trump administrations.
responses.intendedActions:
1. I will use the full platform of the office to keep DC Statehood at the center of the national conversation by building and maintaining a bipartisan congressional coalition, working with state legislators across the country to pass supportive resolutions, and partnering with civil rights, labor, democracy, and good-government organizations to elevate statehood as a national democracy issue. Statehood must be framed not as a local preference, but as unfinished civil rights work and a critical democratic reform.

2. I will actively monitor and respond to congressional riders and oversight efforts that threaten DC’s autonomy. That means coordinated rapid response with the Mayor, Council, Delegate, and regional allies; direct engagement with appropriators; public testimony; and national media advocacy to raise the political cost of federal interference. Congress should not be able to quietly undermine DC’s locally enacted laws.

3. I will treat every major federal debate, from voting rights to reproductive freedom to criminal justice, as connected to DC’s fight. As long as 700,000 residents lack full representation, our democracy remains incomplete.
responses.congressResponse:
If Congress attempts to overturn DC laws or block the District’s budget, I will respond immediately, publicly, and in coordination with every available ally because congressional interference is not just a policy disagreement, it is a denial of democratic self-governance for 700,000 residents.

One specific action I would take is to organize and lead a coordinated federal advocacy push targeting key appropriators and leadership offices the moment a rider or disapproval resolution is introduced. That means direct meetings with members of Congress, mobilizing national civil rights and democracy organizations to apply pressure, and ensuring the issue receives sustained national media attention. Congressional interference often succeeds quietly — I intend to raise the political cost of interference.

I would also work closely with the Mayor, Council, the District’s Delegate to Congress, and my delegation colleagues to present a unified front. When appropriate, I would support litigation strategies to challenge overreach.

Above all, I would make clear that every attempt to override DC law strengthens the moral and political case for Statehood. If Congress insists on governing a city whose residents it does not represent, then it must be prepared to defend that position in full public view.
responses.partners:
Concerned DC Residents and Statehood Advocates: DC residents are the heart of the Statehood movement. As a lifelong Washingtonian, former elected official, and Ward 8 community leader, I have organized alongside neighbors, testified with advocates, and worked in coalition spaces where Statehood has long been a core demand. My relationship with residents and grassroots advocates is not transactional — it’s rooted in shared lived experience. As Senator, I would treat you as essential partners in strategy, mobilization, and movement-building.

National Pro-Democracy Organizations: National pro-democracy and civil rights organizations are essential to framing DC Statehood as a structural democracy issue. In my current role as National Political Director at People For the American Way, I work closely with allied organizations across the country to defend voting rights, civil liberties, and representative government. Those relationships position me to quickly align national messaging, research, grassroots organizing, and federal advocacy efforts around the urgency of Statehood.

Elected Leaders on Capitol Hill and Around the Nation: Building the legislative coalition for Statehood requires sustained engagement with members of Congress and state leaders nationwide. Through my work in national politics and my service as a DC elected official, I have developed relationships with progressive lawmakers, staff, and policy advocates across the country. As Shadow Senator, I would leverage those connections to grow co-sponsors, coordinate public support, and ensure that DC Statehood remains a live and active priority within the broader pro-democracy agenda.
responses.voterInvolvement:
Statehood will not be won solely through congressional maneuvering — it will be won through organized, sustained pressure from DC residents themselves.

1. I will treat the office as an organizing platform, not just an advocacy role. That means hosting regular town halls, ward-based forums, and issue briefings that connect statehood directly to the everyday concerns of residents — housing costs, public safety, reproductive freedom, transportation funding, and protection from federal interference. When people see how lack of representation affects their daily lives, the fight becomes personal and urgent.

2. I will help build and maintain a citywide Statehood coalition that includes civic associations, faith leaders, labor unions, small business owners, students, and neighborhood groups. My goal is to make Statehood visible in every ward — through coordinated days of action, voter education drives, and partnerships with local institutions. We cannot allow Statehood to feel abstract or episodic; it must be woven into the civic culture of the District.

3. I will prioritize youth engagement. Young Washingtonians have often led the moral charge for democracy in this country. By investing in civic education, leadership development, and direct organizing opportunities, we can build the next generation of Statehood advocates who see this as their unfinished work.

4. I will ensure transparency and accountability. Residents deserve regular updates on federal strategy, congressional engagement, and progress. Statehood is a collective effort — and DC voters should feel not like spectators, but like co-authors of the movement that finally secures full representation.
responses.additionalComments:
DC Statehood is not a new position for me, it is the throughline of my public life.

As a student in DC Public Schools, I came to understand early that the decisions shaping my education, my neighborhood, and my future were influenced by members of Congress I could not vote for. That realization didn’t make me cynical. It made me organize. From my earliest days as a youth advocate and student activist, I saw Statehood not as an abstract constitutional debate, but as a question of dignity and equal citizenship.

As an elected member of the DC State Board of Education, I experienced firsthand how vulnerable our local decisions can be to federal interference. And as a national political organizer working to defend democracy across the country, I’ve seen how deeply Americans value representation and self-determination — except, too often, when it comes to the people of their own capital city.

My stance is simple and unwavering: DC deserves full Statehood, full representation, and full control over its budget and laws. Not as a favor. Not as a bargaining chip. But as a matter of fundamental democratic principle.

I am running to be DC’s last Shadow Senator — to help close this chapter in our history and ensure that the next generation of Washingtonians grows up not fighting for equality, but living it.

I had the opportunity to talk with US House Members on both Democrat and Republican about DC issues. They were received positively with continued dialogue on the issues. I have also work with national organizations such as the National Restaurant Association and Main Street American on the important of Statehood.
responses.intendedActions:
As U.S. Shadow Representative, I will take an aggressive and relationship-driven approach to advancing DC Statehood and protecting Home Rule.

First, I will commit to meeting with every single Member of the U.S. House of Representatives at least once during my first term. Building direct relationships across the aisle is essential. I will engage members from both parties to identify common ground—whether it’s taxation, military service, public safety, economic fairness, or democratic principles—and connect those issues back to DC’s lack of full representation.

Second, I will prioritize ongoing conversations with Members of Congress and their staff to ensure DC’s interests are consistently represented. Statehood cannot be a one-time ask; it requires sustained engagement and coalition building.

Third, I will work beyond Capitol Hill by engaging Democratic Parties in other states and encouraging them to include DC Statehood in their platforms. I will ask state and local party leaders to actively advocate with their own Representatives and Senators in support of DC’s full voting rights.

Finally, I will expand national education efforts so that DC Statehood becomes a mainstream American issue—not just a local one. I will pursue opportunities to elevate the cause at major national events, such as the Rose Bowl Parade and the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade, and other large-scale civic gatherings. Millions of Americans tune into these moments. We must use them to tell DC’s story and build public understanding that more than 700,000 taxpaying Americans deserve full representation.
responses.congressResponse:
First, I will organize a coordinated advocacy campaign targeting key Members of Congress, including direct meetings, constituent pressure, and media engagement to oppose the interference. I will work with the Mayor, Council, and national partners to ensure Members understand both the local impact and the broader democratic implications of their actions.

Second, I will hold a press conference and national media briefings to frame the issue clearly: Congressional interference in DC’s local governance is taxation without representation. Elevating the issue nationally is critical to increasing political cost for those attempting to override Home Rule.

Third, I will push for legislative remedies by urging supportive Members of Congress to introduce or reintroduce measures that protect DC’s budget autonomy and limit Congressional micromanagement of local laws.
responses.partners:
First, I intend to work closely with Main Street America. As someone deeply engaged in Main Street corridor revitalization efforts, I understand the power of their national network of local business districts and community development organizations. Main Street America represents communities across the country that believe in local control, economic vitality, and grassroots leadership—values directly aligned with DC’s fight for self-governance.

Second, I plan to partner with the National Restaurant Association. DC’s restaurant industry is a cornerstone of our local economy, and the Association represents thousands of businesses nationwide. Many Members of Congress prioritize restaurant and hospitality issues. I will work to connect the economic strength of DC’s food and beverage sector to the broader argument that the workers and business owners fueling our capital city deserve full representation.

Third, I intend to engage the National Retail Federation. Retailers understand the importance of stable governance, economic predictability, and fair taxation. DC businesses generate billions in economic activity while lacking voting representation in Congress. I will work to elevate that economic fairness argument within the retail community and encourage their advocacy networks to support Statehood.

Today, my relationships with these organizations stem from my work in business corridor revitalization, economic development, and engagement with the restaurant and retail sectors. As Shadow Representative, I will formalize and deepen those partnerships to ensure Statehood is not just a political issue, but a national economic fairness issue.

responses.topThreeActions:
1.) Last year I rallied and marched with the Free DC project, local educators, and local union leaders for Labor Day. We talked about how the lack of statehood affects the quality of education for our children here in DC and their right to an education (albeit a GOOD one). Many of our union leaders talked about how DC is not allowed the right for workers to organize and how this affects union membership and the crumbling workplace protections and standards set in place now. 
2.) I continue to educate those in my circle, whether professional or not, about why DC statehood is so vital. How in particular the lack of statehood keeps many of our black and brown communities disempowered and how their civil rights are fully at the whims of the federal government. This is shown in our over policing and the presence of federal marshals and agents in primarily black neighborhoods. The more these conversations are had, and the more we can connect the dots for those who don’t understand, the more strength and leverage that the people of DC have in our fight.
3.) While this is an unorthodox answer, I believe that it fully aligns with our fight. How can we fight for DC if we are not taking care of the people of DC during this moment? I find myself volunteering in my community, through various means of donations, hands on events, and organizing. Because I feel deep within me that we must set a foundation of care for our communities and those who are most at harm because of the lack of statehood. It builds the bonds of love and trust that will amplify our fight and allow us to truly understand what makes us strong in our unity.
responses.intendedActions:
1.) I intend to hold police and federal agents to the same laws that they are “supposedly” enforcing. Just because we are not a state does not mean this is a playground for brutality or unaccountability. Our communities should know that its government is fighting against the egregious overreach of power.

2.) Create even stricter deadlines for budget reviews, proposed cuts to budget, or changing of laws. We give them too much time to decide on how they are going to hurt us and who is going to be affected the most. We need to add more fuel to that fire. 

3.) I would like to work with abolition groups and organizers/groups that have been here since the beginning of Home Rule and start to draft a constitution. Part of our fight for statehood should affirm what we already know and what we want for DC. We must seize the opportunity when it comes and have our constitution ready to implement to protect our people.
responses.congressResponse:
1.) When it comes to addressing budget short falls, I will fight to ensure our priorities align with working class people. This means that our education, our healthcare and any essential service comes first before surveillance and policing, and that’s how our budget priorities play out.  

2.) NO more tax cuts for billionaires. They will pay their fair share in any form of taxation that we can put upon them. Budget cuts will not be put on working people. Full stop. WE ARE NOT A PLAYGROUND! 
 
3.) I will draft legislation to add more workers protections and adding democracy to our workplace. I will advocate for greater unionization through all industries. One of our biggest bargaining chips against the Trump administration is our labor. Our industry and our workplaces will benefit our communities, not to prop up corrupt politicians.

This moved the conversation from a local political issue to a national civil rights imperative. (https://naacp.org/resources/naacp-reaffirms-support-statehood-and-democratic-right-self-determination-people-district)

By engaging in a non-partisan capacity, I have helped candidates integrate DC Statehood into their own policy platforms.

I will continue to collaborate with civic organizations and administrative bodies to build a nationwide network of voters who will pressure their own representatives to support DC’s rights. Strengthening our administrative presence in civic planning and within the community to ensure that as we grow, our infrastructure is built to state-level standards.

This could look like a Statehood Readiness and Charter Reform Act to work across the aisle with national allies, the growing crowd of litigious non profit organizations and civic organization making it politically and legally expensive for congress to interfere in our local affairs.

responses.voterInvolvement: It is important to humanize the impact...Clearly communicate how specific instances of congressional overreach affect daily life, from school funding to local safety and how statehood would have mitigated those issues. I love data! it's important to equip residents with the data, DC pays more in federal taxes per capita than any other state and has a larger population than both Vermont and Wyoming. I also believe it's important to modernize the argument against DC Statehood... We will workshop responses to hyper-partisan talking points, reminding the country that the Framers of the constitution could not have foreseen a modern, decentralized society where 700,000+ Americans are structurally excluded out of representation.
responses.additionalComments: I want to commend the generations of advocates who have carried this torch. However, the game is evolving, and we must move with it. In a 2026 reality of remote work and decentralized government, the "federal enclave" is a specific footprint not an entire population of 700,000. I am an independent thinker, researcher and a people centric advocate who views statehood as modernization full stop. We are not asking for a favor; we are demanding the return of the rights we already pay more than ever one else for. It is time to align our 18th-century governing documents with our 21st-century reality.
